S-13 is the special case about organizational mirroring; T-05 is broader, also covering direct assertions on calls into internal helpers. They share rule 325, and their legitimate cases are compatible (asserting a call when it IS the specified behavior, per-class test files that assert through the public interface).

coder2.label: HIGHLY SIMILAR
coder2.merged_invariant: A test must express its expectation as a caller-observable result, so that a behavior-preserving refactor cannot change its verdict.
coder2.reason: S-13 requires test organization to follow observable behaviour rather than production's internal structure; T-05 requires a test to assert a caller-observable result so a behaviour-preserving refactor cannot change its verdict. Both rest on rule 325, and T-05 is broader because it also covers assertions on internal call paths (rule 288); both accept per-class test files that still assert through the public interface.

coder1.label: HIGHLY SIMILAR
coder1.merged_invariant: What a boundary publishes must be an enumerated set of names and types that the boundary defines, owns, and makes available to consumers.
coder1.reason: S-24 states that a published surface must be an enumerated set of names the boundary owns and consumers can reach (structural: the boundary does not own its own contract). Y-07 states that every type appearing in a signature across a public boundary must be defined, exported, and published as part of that contract (type laxity: consumers receive an interior type they cannot name). Y-07 is the special case about types in published signatures that are not part of the boundary contract; S-24 is broader, also covering re-export-only files, wildcard re-exports, and persistence entities exposed through service boundaries. They share rules 344 and 448, and their legitimate cases are compatible (facade packages, internal barrels, types exported through another entry point).

coder2.label: HIGHLY SIMILAR
coder2.merged_invariant: What a boundary publishes must be an owned contract, so every type a public signature exposes must itself be a published, owned part of that contract.
coder2.reason: Y-07 requires every type in a signature across a public boundary to be defined, exported and published as part of the contract; S-24 requires what a boundary publishes to be an enumerated set of names the boundary owns. They share rules 344 and 448 (a persistence entity returned, or a signature naming a type kept private), so Y-07 is the type-in-signature case of the broader S-24, which also covers re-export barrels and wildcard exports; both accept an internal boundary whose own model is the contract.

coder3.label: HIGHLY SIMILAR
coder3.merged_invariant: What a boundary publishes must be an enumerated set of names the boundary owns and consumers can reach, every type named in its signatures included.
coder3.reason: Y-07 catches a published signature resting on a type the provider keeps in its interior, an ORM entity returned where a response DTO belongs or an unexported type referenced by an export; S-24 states the wider obligation that a published surface be owned and reachable, holds the same rules 344 and 448, and adds the re-export-only file and the wildcard republication. Both release the same cases: an internal boundary where the interior type genuinely is the contract, and a read model whose entity shape the API documents as its response.

coder3.label: HIGHLY SIMILAR
coder3.merged_invariant: A check the project runs must be made to pass by fixing the code, not by switching that check off or lowering what it demands.
coder3.reason: T-03 watches a failing test being skipped, its assertions lowered or its expectation rewritten to the current output; Y-05 watches a reported type, lint or build diagnostic being suppressed inline or configured away. The two differ only in which check is turned off, and both allow the same disciplined waiver, one whose reason is live and recorded and whose scope is the single case it excuses, which is why rules 207, 208, 210, 332 and 566 sit together in one entry in family I.
